name: Seiso gyaru

lead: Seiso gyaru takes its name from the Japanese word seiso, meaning neat, polished or clean. It is a gyaru substyle that replaced the tanned looks of earlier decades with pale skin, bleached blonde hair, long lashes and decorated nails.
The look helps people present a refined, bright-skinned and groomed appearance through makeup, hair colour and nails. It is tied to a revival of bihaku, the ideal of fair skin, within gyaru culture.

paras: People adopt it through foundation and skincare that keep skin fair, lightened or bleached hair, defined eye makeup with lashes, nail art and a tidy overall outfit. Reiwa-era versions are described as lighter, with smaller lashes and more natural lenses and hair than Heisei-era gyaru.
It is a fashion style with no direct health risk, though bleaching hair, wearing circle lenses and skin-lightening products carry their own usual cautions.

lead: Seiso gyaru, also called seiso-kei, is a substyle of gyaru, the Japanese fashion subculture whose name derives from the English slang word gal [1]. Seiso means neat, polished or clean, and the style is used interchangeably with shiro gyaru [1].

Its signature features are pale skin, bleached blonde hair, elaborate lashes and nail art, a contrast to the tanned styles of the Heisei era [1]. Wikipedia ties it to a revival of bihaku, the ideal of fair, white skin, within gyaru culture [1].

A general gyaru overview lists shiro-gyaru as a substyle that skips the tan and keeps other gyaru elements, often leaning toward cuter styles such as hime gyaru [2]. A separate account of gyaru culture says pale skin is now considered the in thing [3].
infobox: Pale skin, bleached hair, lashes, nail art

paras: Seiso gyaru emphasizes pale skin, bleached blonde hair, elaborate lashes and nail art [1]. Gyaru more broadly features voluminous hair, matte foundation, dramatic lashes and circle lenses, while Reiwa-era makeup is described as lighter with smaller lashes and more natural lenses and hair [1].
The shiro-gyaru label denotes skipping the tan while keeping other gyaru elements, and is often paired with cuter looks [2].

Gyaru grew from 1980s and 1990s youth styles centered on Shibuya, with kogal schoolgirl fashion in the early 1990s and ganguro dark tans in the late 1990s and early 2000s [1][3]. Seiso gyaru was coined during the 2010s decline of the subculture, alongside labels such as neo gyaru [1].

Print magazines such as egg, Popteen, Ranzuki and Koakuma Ageha drove earlier eras, and social media largely replaced print in the Reiwa era [1]. The magazine egg ended print publication in 2014 and later returned online, with periodic print issues [3].
